domain: Storm God, Lord of the Heavens
meaning: Canaanite storm and fertility god; the title "Lord" (baʿlu) was also applied to local deities

phonemes.desc: Plain voiced bilabial [b] plus open [a]; the word means 'lord, owner, husband' across Semitic languages.
Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] plus [a] and [l]. The pharyngeal is the signature consonant; we render it with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for registrability.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-ahl' — the middle consonant is a deep, throaty 'ʿ' (like Arabic ع), not a glottal stop or silent letter.

kin.label: Ugaritic
kin.form: 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl), 'lord'; as divine name often paired with Hadad/Haddu, the storm/thunder god

kin.label: Hebrew
kin.form: בַּעַל (Baʿal), 'lord, husband'; later a polemical name for Canaanite gods

kin.label: Akkadian
kin.form: Adad/Hadad (dIM), the storm god with whom Baꜥal was equated

pronunciation.note: Baꜥal is technically a title ('Lord') that became a name. The ideal form includes Semitic ʿayin, which is blocked at the DNS root; the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) is the registrable compromise. The name is Tier 2 because it preserves the ʿayin as a distinctive phoneme but carries no stress or length mark. In texts he is often 'Baꜥlu-Haddu' or simply the 'Rider on the Clouds.'

domains.title: Rider on the Clouds
domains.subtitle: Storm, Fertility, and Divine Kingship
domains.lead: Baꜥal is the storm made king. In a land where rain is life and drought is death, he is the deity who rides the clouds, shatters the sea-monster, and opens his palace windows so that the rains may fall. He is young, vigorous, and hungry for a throne — yet even his kingship depends on the older god Ēl. The Baꜥal Cycle is the great myth of his rise, death, and return.

cards.name: Storm and Thunder
cards.desc: His voice is thunder, his weapon lightning; he gathers clouds, wind, and rain around his chariot.

cards.name: Lord of Mount Zaphon
cards.desc: His cedar palace stands on the mountain of the north, the axis mundi from which he governs the cosmos.

cards.name: Fertility of Field and Flock
cards.desc: When he lives, bread, wine, and oil abound; when he descends to Mot, the land withers.

cards.name: Divine Warrior
cards.desc: He defeats Yamm, the primordial Sea, and shatters the seven-headed serpent Lotan.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: His father's animal and a sign of fertility and storm power

symbols.name: Lightning club
symbols.meaning: The divine weapon forged by Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs

symbols.name: Window
symbols.meaning: The palace window through which Baꜥal's thunder and rain go forth to the world

symbols.name: Cloud chariot
symbols.meaning: His vehicle, the storm cloud itself

mythology.lead: The Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) is the central myth of Canaanite religion. It tells how Baꜥal wins kingship from the chaotic Sea, builds his palace, confronts Death, and returns to bring back the rains. The cycle is a seasonal drama of drought and renewal, but also a political statement about divine legitimacy.

myths.title: Baꜥal and Yamm
myths.text: Ēl grants kingship to Yamm, the Sea, who sends messengers demanding that Baꜥal be delivered as a slave. Baꜥal refuses. The craftsman god Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs forges two clubs, Yagrush ('Chaser') and Ayamur ('Driver'). With them Baꜥal strikes Yamm on the skull and scatters the chaotic waters, claiming the throne for himself (KTU 1.2 iv).

myths.title: The Palace on Zaphon
myths.text: Victorious, Baꜥal still has no palace. He sends ꜥAnat to petition Ēl, but it is Asherah who finally secures permission. Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs builds a cedar palace on Mount Zaphon. Baꜥal hesitates over a window — it will let his voice out, but it may also let Death in. He opens it, and his thunder resounds across the earth (KTU 1.3–1.4).

myths.title: Descent into Mot
myths.text: Death, personified as Mot, invites Baꜥal to the underworld. Baꜥal descends with his clouds, winds, and rains; the earth dries up. His sisters ꜥAnat and Aštart mourn him, and ꜥAnat destroys Mot, scattering his body like seed. Baꜥal returns, the rains resume, and fertility is restored (KTU 1.5–1.6).

myths.title: Protector of Ugarit
myths.text: A ritual prayer from Ugarit (KTU 1.119) invokes Baꜥal to drive the enemy from the city gates and walls. Votive anchors from his temple show his importance to seafarers; having conquered Yamm, he protects those who sail the waters he once defeated.

lore.syncretism: Baꜥal is inseparable from the older West Semitic storm god Hadad/Haddu; in texts and inscriptions the two names are often combined as Baꜥal-Haddu. In Mesopotamia he was equated with Adad (dIM), and in Egypt he influenced the Levantine storm god imported during the New Kingdom. The Greeks saw in him a Near Eastern Zeus, a sky-storm king, though they did not directly worship him. In the Hebrew Bible, Baꜥal became the archetype of apostasy, the 'false god' opposed by Elijah on Mount Carmel. Later Jewish and Christian tradition demonized the name, turning 'Baal' into a byword for idolatry and, in medieval occultism, for a class of demons.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Canaanite name was more reviled or more enduring than Baꜥal. The prophets of Israel spent generations attacking his cult, yet his imagery — the storm god who rides the clouds, defeats the sea, and sends rain — was quietly absorbed into the figure of Yahweh. In the New Testament, Beelzebub ('Lord of the Flies,' probably a distortion of Baꜥal-Zebul, 'Prince Baꜥal') becomes a name for Satan. In modern fantasy and occult literature, Baal persists as a demon-king. But beneath the polemic remains the old Levantine truth: a god of storm and fertility whose absence means drought and whose return means life.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Baꜥal is the god of the necessary storm. He does not create the world; he saves it from chaos, builds a house for his voice, and dies so that the cycle of rain may continue. His mythology is not about transcendence but about recurrence — the eternal return of the waters that make civilization possible.

In a warming world, Baꜥal's story takes on new weight. The storm is no longer merely symbolic; it is the weather that either nourishes or destroys. To remember Baꜥal is to remember that divine kingship, in the ancient imagination, was bound to the rains. The health of the cosmos and the legitimacy of the king rose and fell together. That is a theology we have not outgrown, however much we have renamed it.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (b-ʿ-l), literally 'lord.' The middle sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative. Because Semitic ʿayin is blocked at the DNS root, PUNYCODEX renders it with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724). In many contexts the name is an appellative rather than a personal name; at Ugarit the storm god is often called Baꜥlu-Haddu.

lore.archaeology: The Temple of Baal at Ugarit, excavated by Claude Schaeffer, yielded stelae, votive anchors, and the Baʿal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6). The Karatepe bilingual pairs Baʿal with King Azatiwada in Phoenician and Luwian. At Palmyra the great Temple of Baal-Shamin dominated the city; at Carthage, Baʿal-Hammon received child sacrifice in the tophet sanctuary. Hazor, Megiddo, and Mount Carmel provide Levantine cultic contexts attacked by biblical polemic.
